# Stationary mixed cuts: exact section-centroid and balancing formulas

This note treats d>=1 and ordinary mixed d-volume. It establishes the
first-variation identities under their exact regularity conditions, and
records two explicit obstructions to stronger section-based assertions.
No mixed-integer Grünbaum inequality is invoked.

Let C be a compact convex body in R^n x R^d. Write K_z=C_z and let Z_+
be the finite set of z for which |K_z|_d>0. The original mixed volume is

    mu(A)=sum_{z in Z_+}|A_z|_d.

Fibers of zero d-volume make no contribution to this measure. Fix
z_0 with K_z0 of positive volume, and x_0 in its interior. For a in R^n
and b in R^d with |b|=1, define

    F(a,b;x_0)=sum_z |{x in K_z:
        a dot(z-z_0)+b dot(x-x_0)>=0}|_d.         (1)

These are exactly the cuts through y=(z_0,x_0) with nonzero continuous
normal, normalized to unit continuous normal.

## 1. Compact reduction of the normal parameters

For x_0 in a fixed compact neighborhood, there is a finite R such that
minimizing (1) over a in R^n, |b|=1 is equivalent to minimizing it over
|a|<=R, |b|=1. Moreover that minimum is attained.

Here is an explicit finite-dimensional argument. Put r_z=z-z_0. Since
all fibers and the neighborhood of x_0 are bounded, choose B so that
|b dot(x-x_0)|<=B for every fiber point and every unit b. For a given
a,b, classify each fiber cap as full, empty, or partial. On each partial
fiber, the value a dot r_z belongs to [-B,B]; impose the equality

    a' dot r_z=a dot r_z.

On each full fiber impose the corresponding weak lower bound on
 a' dot r_z which guarantees fullness; on each empty fiber impose the
weak upper bound guaranteeing zero d-volume. The right sides of all
these equations and inequalities have magnitude at most B. The
original a is feasible. Passing from strict emptiness to a boundary
plane changes no d-volume because b is nonzero.

All coefficient rows belong to the fixed finite family {r_z,-r_z}.
Take the feasible point of minimum Euclidean norm. It exists because
the feasible polyhedron is nonempty and closed. Its vector lies in the
span of its active coefficient rows: otherwise subtracting a small
component perpendicular to those rows preserves the active equations
and the strict inactive inequalities while decreasing its norm.
Choose independent active rows spanning this vector, arranged as a
matrix A_I. The minimum-norm point is therefore

    a'=A_I^T(A_I A_I^T)^(-1)c_I.

There are only finitely many possible independent row sets, and all
entries of c_I have magnitude at most B. Their displayed operator norms
give a uniform finite R. The rank-zero case has a'=0. This a' preserves
every partial-fiber cap and every full/empty fiber volume, so it
preserves F exactly.

For |b|=1, every bounding plane has d-dimensional measure zero in each
fiber. Dominated convergence therefore makes F continuous in a,b,x_0.
The bounded normal domain is compact, proving attainment.

Vertical cuts do not reduce the infimum. Given a vertical cut through
y, choose any unit b and replace its integer normal a by T a. For all
large T, every fiber with a dot r_z nonzero is included or excluded
exactly as before, because there are only finitely many bounded fibers.
Every tied fiber was entirely in the original closed vertical cut and
is only partially retained by the new cut. Thus a nonvertical cut has
mass no greater. Consequently the attained nonvertical minimum equals
the full halfspace depth at y, multiplied by total mass.

The same R can be used on a compact neighborhood of x_0, which is
useful for the local-maximum argument below.

## 2. First variation of a regular cut

For a given a,b define its section in each positive-volume fiber by

    L_z={x in K_z:a dot r_z+b dot(x-x_0)=0}.

Assume the section has zero (d-1)-measure on the boundary of K_z:

    H_{d-1}(L_z intersect boundary K_z)=0
    for every z in Z_+.                          (2)

This includes all transverse sections. It also includes tangencies to
strictly convex fibers when d>=2, since such a contact is a point and
has zero H_{d-1} measure. In d=1, a cut at an interval endpoint is
excluded by (2). Positive-area exposed facets lying in the cut are
also excluded. Smoothness is not otherwise required for this formula.

Under (2), the directional derivative is

    D F[(delta a,delta b)]
      =sum_{z in Z_+} integral_Lz
          [delta a dot r_z+delta b dot(x-x_0)]
          dH_{d-1}(x),                           (3)

where b has unit length; for an unnormalized b the right side is divided
by |b|. The derivative with respect to the chosen point in its fiber is

    D_x0 F[h]=-s(a,b) b dot h,
    s(a,b)=sum_{z in Z_+} H_{d-1}(L_z).           (4)

To justify these formulas directly, rotate the continuous coordinates
so that b is the last coordinate vector. A nearby cut can be solved
as a graph for the last coordinate, because its coefficient remains
nonzero. Sections of K_z parallel to that coordinate are intervals.
The retained interval length is differentiated wherever the cut graph
is strictly between its endpoints; at points outside it the derivative
is zero. Condition (2) removes the exceptional endpoint graph on a set
of (d-1)-measure zero. The graph's derivative is exactly the linear
expression in (3). The bodies and perturbations are bounded, providing
an integrable uniform bound. Fubini and dominated convergence give
(3), and the same calculation for a moving x_0 gives (4). Empty or
zero-area sections contribute zero. There are only finitely many
fibers, so differentiating their sum is legitimate.

## 3. A minimizing normal forces the derivative section's centroid

Suppose (a,b), |b|=1, globally or locally minimizes F over the full
normal family and obeys (2). Variation of a in every direction gives

    sum_z H_{d-1}(L_z)(z-z_0)=0.                 (5)

Variation of b in its unit-sphere tangent space shows that

    V=sum_z integral_Lz(x-x_0)dH_{d-1}(x)

is parallel to b. Every section point obeys
 b dot(x-x_0)=-a dot(z-z_0); integrating and using (5) yields b dot V=0.
Thus V=0. Since the central fiber contains x_0 in its interior, its
section has positive (d-1)-measure (counting measure one when d=1), so
s(a,b)>0. Therefore the finite positive measure

    sigma_{a,b}=sum_{z in Z_+} H_{d-1}|_{ {z} x L_z }

has its full ambient centroid exactly at y=(z_0,x_0).

Crucially this measure includes only the d-positive fibers. It equals
the full intrinsic H_{d-1} section measure only if all other section
fibers have zero H_{d-1} measure. This restriction cannot be dropped;
see the first obstruction below.

## 3a. Exact lattice-preserving identification of the section

Rotate only the continuous coordinates so that b is the final coordinate
vector. The cut plane is then x_d=x_0d-a dot(z-z_0). The affine shear

    (z,x_1,...,x_d) ->
    (z,x_1,...,x_(d-1),x_d+a dot(z-z_0)-x_0d)

preserves Z^n x R^d and maps the section to the last-coordinate-zero
plane. On each fixed integer fiber it is a translation after an
orthogonal rotation. It therefore preserves that fiber's H_(d-1)
section measure, and hence the finite sum of those measures exactly.
Identifying the last-coordinate-zero plane with R^n x R^(d-1) produces
a convex section body in the correct smaller mixed space.

This section body is full-dimensional in its new ambient space: the
cut passes through the interior of the central positive fiber, so C
has points on both sides of the plane. Mixing these points slightly
with an ambient interior point supplies ambient interior points of both
signs, whose segment meets the plane in ambient interior. Thus the
relative section has dimension n+d-1 and nonempty relative interior.

If all original nonempty fibers have positive d-volume, the section
measure in the preceding centroid identity is precisely the induced
mixed (d-1)-volume of this smaller body. Otherwise a formerly zero-volume
fiber may acquire positive section measure; that is exactly the defect
in Section 5. This coordinate identification supplies no depth inequality
for the section centroid by itself.

## 4. Balanced active cuts at an interior depth maximum

Suppose x_0 is a local maximum of the halfspace depth within the
interior of K_z0. Suppose all minimizing normal parameters in the
compact reduction satisfy (2), and the derivatives (3)-(4) are
continuous on a neighborhood of that compact active family. Smooth
strictly convex positive fibers in dimension d>=2 are one sufficient
setting; in dimension one the active cuts must stay away from interval
endpoints.

Then there are at most d+1 minimizing cuts (a_j,b_j) and positive
weights theta_j with

    sum_j theta_j b_j=0, sum_j theta_j=1.          (6)

Each cut's derivative section has ambient centroid y by the preceding
section. To prove (6), first consider their gradients -s_j b_j in (4).
If zero is outside their compact convex hull, strict separation gives
a direction h with all active gradients dot h positive, uniformly.
Derivative continuity preserves this improvement on a neighborhood of
the active parameter set. Its compact complement has a uniform positive
gap above the minimizing mass. Uniform continuity, or the uniform
section-volume Lipschitz bound for moving x_0, preserves that gap for
small movements. Hence moving x_0 slightly along h would increase the
minimum of every cut mass, contradicting the local maximum.

Thus zero belongs to the convex hull of the active gradients. The
finite-dimensional convex-hull theorem gives at most d+1 of them and
nonnegative coefficients. Discard zero coefficients and absorb their
positive section masses s_j into the weights. This proves (6), because
s_j>0 for every active cut through the interior central-fiber point.

The regularity and compactness assumptions in this section are stated
explicitly. Nonsmooth active cuts and positive boundary-section mass
require subdifferentials or separate limiting arguments not supplied
here.

## 5. Exact failure of the full intrinsic-section centroid assertion

Take n=1,d=2 and

    C=conv( {0} x unit disk,
            {1} x ([-1,1] x {0}) ).

This is a full-dimensional compact convex body in R^3. Its only integer
fibers are the unit disk at z=0 and the horizontal segment at z=1.
Mixed H_2 volume lives only on the disk. At y=(0,0,0), every nonvertical
cut through y has half the disk area, so H={x_2>=0} is a globally
minimizing cut and its full-normal first derivative is zero.

The derivative section consists of the central disk's horizontal
diameter, length two, whose centroid is y. But the full H_1 section
also includes the length-two segment at z=1. Its integer-coordinate
centroid is 1/2, not z_0=0. Thus stationarity does not imply that the
full intrinsic section has centroid y when zero-d-volume fibers become
positive section fibers. Smooth strict convexity of every positive-
volume fiber does not repair this example.

## 6. Even balanced global minimizers need not have a concave profile

Take instead

    C=[-1,1] x unit disk, y=(0,0,0),
    H={3z+x_2>=0}.

All three integer fibers are positive-volume smooth strictly convex
unit disks. The induced mixed set is centrally symmetric about y.
Every through-y nonvertical cut has exactly half the total mixed mass,
since its boundary has zero H_2 measure and reflection exchanges its
two sides. Consequently H and its opposite are global minimizing cuts
with a balanced pair of continuous normals.

At the cut level zero, only the central fiber meets the plane: its
section is the horizontal diameter. Its full section centroid is y.
The same is true for the opposite cut.

Nevertheless the parallel mixed section profile is exactly

    P(t)=2 sum_{z=-1,0,1} sqrt(1-(t-3z)^2)_+,

where the summand is defined as zero whenever |t-3z|>1. Its positive
support has three disjoint components (-4,-2),(-1,1),(2,4). For example
P(0)=P(3)=2 but P(3/2)=0. It is therefore not log-concave, and no
positive power of it is concave on its support's convex hull.

This obstruction satisfies the section-centroid identity, a balanced
family, globally minimizing cuts, an interior fiber point, and smooth
positive fibers. It disproves the precise auxiliary claim that these
conditions make the summed parallel-section profile eligible for an
ordinary one-dimensional Brunn-Minkowski/Prékopa induction. Each
individual fiber profile still has its usual power concavity; their
integer sum does not inherit it.

The example has depth one half, so it is not a counterexample to OC.

## 7. A stronger obstruction: connected profile and all-level centroids

The preceding disconnected support is not essential. Consider

    C=conv( {0} x disk(radius 2),
            {-1,1} x disk(radius 1) ).

Equivalently C={|z|<=1, |x|+|z|<=2}, so this is explicitly a compact
full-dimensional convex body. Its integer fibers have radii 1,2,1.
Every fiber is positive, smooth, and strictly convex. The set is
centrally symmetric, so y=(0,0,0) is again a global halfspace-depth
one-half center, and H={x_2>=0} together with its opposite is a balanced
pair of globally minimizing cuts.

For every t with |t|<2, the parallel section x_2=t has full ambient
centroid (0,0,t): the two outer integer fibers have equal section
lengths whenever present, the central fiber has integer coordinate
zero, all horizontal intervals are centered at x_1=0, and x_2=t is
constant. This is an all-level centroid identity, not just stationarity
at one selected cut.

The exact parallel mixed profile is

    P(t)=2 sqrt((4-t^2)_+)+4 sqrt((1-t^2)_+).

It is continuous, even, and decreasing for t>=0, with connected positive
support (-2,2). Nevertheless it is not log-concave. Indeed,

    P(1)^2=12,
    P(3/4)=sqrt(55)/2+sqrt(7)>6,
    P(5/4)=sqrt(39)/2>3.

The strict bounds use only 55>7^2, 7>(5/2)^2, and 39>6^2. Therefore

    P(1)^2 < P(3/4)P(5/4),

contradicting the midpoint inequality for log-concavity. In particular
no positive power of P is concave: positive-power concavity would imply
this log-concavity inequality by the arithmetic-geometric mean
inequality.

Thus neither connectedness, symmetry, unimodality, nor the stronger
centroid identity at every parallel level repairs the summed-profile
obstruction. The original mixed set still has depth one half, so this
is solely an exact counterexample to the proposed profile-concavity
invariant.
